paper_title: Rethinking Video Storage for AI Training: Breaking Cross-Frame Dependencies for Efficient Random Access

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large-scale AI training increasingly relies on massive video datasets with random temporal sampling patterns. However, existing video storage paradigms are optimized for sequential playback and employ sophisticated inter-frame reference structures to maximize compression efficiency. When applied to the random-sampling workloads of AI training, these paradigms face substantial decoding-efficiency bottlenecks. Workarounds such as independent JPEG frames and short groups of pictures (GOPs) reduce decoding work at the cost of larger storage and transfer volumes. In this paper, we identify two sources of decode amplification: sequential reconstruction of unrelated frames and reconstruction of the reference chains required by sampled targets. We address both sources by co-designing the decoding schedule and video reference structure. Dependency-aware sparse decoding reconstructs only requested frames and their required references, skipping unrelated reconstruction without transcoding the source videos. Optional offline Dependency-Decoupled Random Access (DDRA) encoding further reduces reference reconstruction by restricting each interior frame to two bounding intra-coded anchors. Together, sparse decoding and DDRA retain inter-frame prediction while bounding reconstruction to at most three frames per requested target, independent of the intra period. Experiments on a large-scale robotics corpus show that, at comparable reconstruction quality, our method achieves $1.45\times$ the loading throughput of LeRobot v3 with 58.7% less media payload.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Video-based learning systems are increasingly used in autonomous driving, robotics [2, 9, 29, 32], and multimodal understanding [4, 30, 31]. Instead of sequential playback, the training workloads repeatedly sample short windows or sparse frames from long recordings, shuffle requests across videos, and revisit the corpus over many epochs. An effective storage path must therefore combine compact representation with fine-grained temporal access and sustained data delivery to accelerators; sequential throughput alone is insufficient. Conventional video storage exposes compressionrandom-access tension under these workloads. Generalpurpose video codecs exploit inter-frame redundancy to reduce storage and transfer volume [24, 26], but their playback-oriented designs introduce two sources of decode amplification. First, container-level seeking locates synchronization point but does not make decoding frame-selective: conventional pipelines decode every intervening frame sequentially until the target is produced, even though many of these frames are not requested by the training workload. Second, hierarchical reference structures allow frames to depend on other frames, so producing one target may additionally require reconstructing transitive chain of reference frames. Together, redundant sequential decoding and mandatory reference reconstruction consume CPU time without directly producing requested training samples. Materializing every frame as an independently compressed image avoids temporal decode dependencies, and 1 rowor shard-based formats can then expose individual images to sampler [13, 21]. more storage-efficient compromise uses mini-GOP video coding to shorten reference dependency chains, as in our LeRobot [3] baseline. Both representations better match sparse access, but they sacrifice inter-frame redundancyeither entirely or through frequent intra-coded anchorsand thereby increase persistent-storage use and network-bandwidth demand during training. We address this tension by co-designing the online decoding schedule and the offline video representation around training requests. First, dependency-aware sparse decoding reconstructs only the requested frames and their direct and transitive references in dependency-respecting order, skipping unrelated frames that sequential decoder would otherwise process. This removes redundant decoding, but leaves the required reference chains intact. To shorten these chains, we introduce Dependency-Decoupled Random Access (DDRA), an offline encoding configuration that removes B-to-B reference edges and restricts each interior frame to the two intra-coded anchors that bound its intra period. The resulting dependency closure contains only the target and its two anchors. Together, sparse decoding and DDRA reduce both sources of decode amplification while retaining inter-frame prediction, standards-compliant bitstreams, and the decoded-frame interface expected by existing training pipelines. We evaluate two settings on three robotics datasets comprising 3,000 episodes and 8,908 camera streams  (Table 1)  . Without offline transcoding, our sparse loader is 1.81, 1.34, and 1.25 faster than PyAV, Decord, and TorchCodec, respectively, based on average loading time across four access patterns. With offline transcoding at comparable reconstruction quality, our H.265 variant achieves 1.45 the throughput of LeRobot v3 and 2.02 that of JPEG, while reducing media payload by 58.7% and 90.0%, respectively. Figure 1 summarizes this storagethroughput trade-off using the same average loading times. Our contributions are threefold: We analyze the video-storage requirements of AI training and identify two sources of decode amplification: sequential decoding of unrelated frames and transitive frame dependencies. We combine dependency-aware sparse decoding with DDRA encoding, eliminating unrelated frame reconstruction and bounding each interior targets dependency closure while retaining inter-frame prediction. Experiments across three datasets and four access patterns demonstrate faster native video loading and, after quality-aligned transcoding, higher throughput with less media payload than LeRobot v3 and JPEG. Figure 1 Storagethroughput trade-off for different storage methods. The ratio of p95 to mean loading time.

sections.title: 2.1 Video Coding Framework
sections.content: General video coding frameworks combine carefully designed modules to exploit different forms of redundancy. Spatial prediction and transform coding reduce correlations within frame; quantization controls reconstruction precision, and entropy coding exploits statistical regularities in the coded symbols. Temporal redundancy is typically dominant because neighboring frames share much of their visual content [17]. Inter-frame prediction exploits this overlap through motion compensation from reconstructed reference pictures, so only motion vectors and residual differences need to be coded [24, 26]. This temporal compression introduces dependencies between pictures. pictures use no inter-frame prediction and can be reconstructed independently of other pictures. In conventional prediction structures, pictures depend on earlier reference pictures, whereas pictures may use both earlier and later references in presentation order. sections.title: 2.2 Existing Data Organizations and Pipelines
sections.content: Training pipelines locate sampled observations and fetch the corresponding visual data, which is decoded and augmented before being passed to the GPU as RGB tensors (Figure 2, upper left). Dataset formats support this process through different data organizations. For example, WebDataset packs objects into shards for sequential access [1]. Parquet stores tabular records, whereas Lance supports random access to multimodal data [21]. Data organization determines how samples are located and accessed, while visual encoding influences the cost of transferring and decoding them. During training, such data must first be transferred from storage to compute nodes and then decoded into RGB tensors. In this context, both I/O and decoding can become bottlenecks. These two costs lead to compressionaccess trade-off. Inter-frame coding reduces transfer volume by exploiting temporal redundancy, but accessing sampled frame may require reconstructing additional reference frames. Independently coded frames remove these dependencies but require larger payload (Figure 2, lower right). Short groups of pictures (GOPs) provide compromise, retaining temporal compression while shortening reference chains. For example, our LeRobot v3 [3] baseline uses AV1 with two-frame GOP. Our approach improves this trade-off by co-designing the encoded reference structure and the decoding schedule for sparse training requests. 1https://github.com/PyAV-Org/PyAV/tree/v18.1.0 2https://github.com/meta-pytorch/torchcodec/tree/v0.7.0 3https://github.com/dmlc/decord/tree/v0.6.0 3 Figure 2 Codecloader co-design for video-based training. Optional offline DDRA encoding and online dependency-aware sparse decoding deliver requested RGB frames. (a) Hierarchical coding requires intermediate B-frame references; (b) DDRA coding restricts each interior frame to two intra-coded anchors, reducing the illustrated dependency closure. Related systems also reduce loading overhead through more efficient data delivery, storage, and reuse. FFCV streamlines loading and preprocessing [13], while Progressive Compressed Records allow training to use different image fidelities [11]. Caching systems such as CoorDL, Quiver, SHADE, and Seneca reduce repeated data access [6, 10, 12, 19], and SAND enables reuse of preprocessing outputs for video training [28]. Video storage systems also optimize how the data is represented and accessed: VStore selects formats for analytics, VSS manages layouts and caches, and TASM uses tiling for spatial access [5, 8, 27]. Our approach complements these efforts by reducing cost for transferring and decoding when no previous results are unavailable for reuse.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: Our approach co-designs the decoding schedule and the encoding reference graph to reduce the two components of decode amplification in Equation 3. Online dependency-aware sparse decoding removes most of the unrelated reconstruction. Optional offline DDRA encoding further reduces the reference frames by restricting the reference frames of each B-frame to two intra-coded anchors. Figure 2 shows how the two components fit into the training data path.

sections.title: 3.1 Dependency-Aware Sparse Decoding
sections.content: Video containers typically store coded frames as individually addressable samples, making selective frame access possible. To respect the reference dependencies in Section 2.1, selective reconstruction must include the closure D(Q) defined in Equation 2. Given requested indices with distinct-frame set Q, we first perform header-parsing pass to construct the reference graph. We select segment from preceding random-access anchor through the last target in decoding order, extending it backward if required references are unavailable (Appendix A.4). For each frame , we define Ref(f ) as the union of the active reference lists across its slice headers. breadth-first traversal from then yields the dependency closure D(Q) (Equation 2). We then traverse in decoding order, reconstructing each frame in D(Q) once and skipping pixel reconstruction for the remaining frames 4 Algorithm 1 Dependency-aware sparse decoding with validated reference graph Input: Encoded video , decoding order π, requested indices q. This order ensures that references are reconstructed before their dependent pictures. Only frames in are converted to RGB, and the outputs are returned in the original request order, including duplicates (Algorithm 1). Skipping reconstruction still requires preserving the decoder state σ. For each skipped frame, state-only path updates picture-order counts and reference management in the decoded picture buffer (DPB) to maintain consistency with the encoders DPB state. On validated reference graph, the schedule thus satisfies Rπ(Q) = D(Q) and removes unrelated reconstruction. The remaining decoding cost is determined by the frame-reference structure, motivating DDRA.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate data loading performance on corpus consisting of 3,000 episodes and 8,908 camera streams curated from RealSourceWorld, RoboCasa [20], and Table30v2 [18]. All loading experiments store every representation as episode-level Lance records on OSS (object storage) and read it through this common storage path. PyAV, Decord, TorchCodec, and Ours native consume the original bitstreams without transcoding; Ours native uses dependency-aware sparse decoding. The transcoded baselines are LeRobot v3 [3] and JPEG. LeRobot v3 does not mandate particular video codec; we use its recommended configuration4 for this comparison. Ours-DDRA (H.264/H.265) uses bitstreams with open GOPs and intra period TI = 32. We first validate sparse decoding correctness through pixelwise comparison with full sequential decoding (Appendix A.5). Our evaluation then examines efficiency, training performance, and operating limits. We compare loading time and storage cost across methods (Section 4.2). We then evaluate how training-data compression affects VLA, WAM, and VLM task performance (Section 4.3). We also vary temporal sampling and loader resources to assess the robustness of loading speedup, constrain OSS bandwidth to identify transferlimited regimes, and sweep the intra period to characterize the loading-timepayload trade-off (Section 4.4). Detailed experimental protocols are provided in Appendices AD.

4.2 Loading Efficiency and Storage Cost
Loading results. All methods use one 16-CPU, 64-GiB node, 32 workers, and batch size eight. The timed path
covers OSS reads, RGB decoding, and metadata return (Appendix A.3). Sparse decoding improves average
loading time in all four patterns without changing the stored video (Table 1). Averaged across patterns, Ours
native is 1.81×, 1.34×, and 1.25× faster than PyAV, Decord, and TorchCodec, respectively. It also has the
lowest native p95 in all patterns except for Stride-2. DDRA transcoding further improves loading efficiency.
In random access mode, the H.264 and H.265 DDRA representations reduce average loading time from 297.8
to 134.1 and 140.6 ms/batch, respectively (2.22× and 2.12×). Both have lower mean and p95 loading times
than LeRobot v3 and JPEG in every main-table pattern.
sections.content: Payloadthroughput trade-off. Among methods requiring offline transcoding, Ours-DDRA reduces media payload for better storage/transmission efficiency and improves batch loading throughput at aligned quality (Figure 1). Its H.264/H.265 representations provide 1.421.45 LeRobot v3s throughput with 29.858.7% less media payload, and 1.992.02 JPEGs throughput with 83.090.0% less payload. H.265 requires less storage than H.264 while achieving comparable loading times. We therefore use H.265 for the subsequent training-performance evaluation.

sections.title: 4.3 Training Performance under Compression
sections.content: We evaluate how DDRA compression affects downstream performance for VLA and WAM on LIBERO [16] and VLM on MVBench [14], with fixed training budgets within each model family. The VLA and VLM 7 Figure 4 Training performance under compression. DDRA (H.265) approximately halves storage and bandwidth requirements relative to LeRobot v3 at comparable VLA/WAM performance, while high-quality transcoding need not reduce VLM accuracy. Compression factors use the original visual representations as anchors, explaining their different ranges. experiments use π0.5 [22] and Qwen3.5-2B, respectively. Our WAM experiments follow OpenWAM [25]. Figure 4 compares task performance against the compression factor relative to Original. Appendix provides the protocols and numerical results. DDRA (H.265) requires approximately 50% less storage and media-transfer bandwidth than LeRobot v3 while maintaining comparable VLA and WAM performance. Following the procedure in prior work Liang et al. [15], we compute approximate 95% confidence intervals for the success-rate (SR) differences of LeRobot v3 and DDRA relative to Original. Under this approximation, DDRA (H.265) shows no statistically significant SR change for either VLA or WAM at approximately 100 compression relative to Original (p > 0.05; Appendix B.3). For VLM, transcoding does not necessarily reduce downstream accuracy when video quality remains high. One possible explanation is that moderate compression brings the visual distribution of the training videos closer to that of the test videos.

sections.content: Access and Resource Sensitivity. DDRAs loading gains persist across all 27 tested access/resource configurations (selected settings in Figure 7 of Appendix C). Varying requested frame count, stride, random span, batch size, workers, and CPU allocation gives speedups over Ours native of 1.444.41 for H.264 and 1.593.27 for H.265. The one-variable sweeps use 100 measured batches per point; Appendix gives their settings and scaling analysis. Influence of Intra-period. However, the greater temporal distance to these anchors can make inter-frame prediction less efficient and increase the total bitrate. Component Ablation. Table 2 quantifies the incremental gains of sparse decoding and DDRA encoding in the proposed pipeline. All three configurations use H.265 with TI = 32, identical sampled requests, and the same loading resources (Appendix A). Sequential decodes each requested intra period in coding order through its last target, skipping untouched periods and unused tails. The first comparison keeps the encoded videos unchanged and replaces sequential reconstruction with sparse decoding. The second keeps sparse decoding enabled and measures the additional benefit of the DDRA encoding configuration. Each stage reduces reconstruction work and loading time across all three access patterns. Under random access, sparse decoding reduces reconstructed frames from 233.9 to 92.3 per episode and batch-loading time from 668.3 to 297.8 ms, yielding 2.24 speedup. Adding DDRA further reduces these values to 43.1 frames per episode and 134.1 ms per batch, yielding an additional 2.22 speedup over sparse decoding alone. The frame counts support the intended reduction in reconstruction work, while the timings quantify the incremental loading benefit of each stage. Across patterns, the combined design achieves 2.734.98 speedup over Sequential.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: This paper explores workload-aware video storage for AI training. By modifying codec reference structures, DDRA bridges efficient compression and efficient random access. On our controlled three-dataset benchmark, Ours-DDRA (H.264) and (H.265) reduce average loading time in random access mode by 2.22 and 2.12, respectively, relative to native sparse H.264 loading. Across four access patterns they achieve sampled-episode loading throughputs of 64.66 and 65.75 ep/s while using 83.090.0% less media payload than JPEG. These results show that bounded reference dependencies provide practical operating point between playbackoriented compression and image-oriented random access. The preferred representation depends on request span and bandwidth; the reported loading rates do not establish full-tensor delivery rates or training-time speedups.

sections.title: A Loading Benchmark Details
sections.content: A.1 Corpus, Sampling, and Implementations The loading corpus retains every camera and the full duration of all 3,000 episodes. RealSourceWorld and RoboCasa each contribute 3,000 camera streams; Table30v2 contributes 2,908. All methods use the same deterministic episode order and target indices. The episode order follows shuffled full-dataset cycles, visiting each datasets 1,000 episodes before starting its next cycle. Each request selects ten frames per camera. Contiguous uses consecutive timesteps; Stride-2 and Stride-4 use the corresponding fixed temporal stride. In random access mode (labeled Random in Table 1), we first select deterministic 100-frame window, then sample ten frames without replacement and sort their indices. For episodes shorter than 100 frames, the candidate set is the available episode; samples are neither dropped nor padded. All representations use episode-level Lance on OSS (Section 4.1). Original retains the dataset-provided H.264 MP4 payload without transcoding. PyAV seeks to each requested intra period and decodes sequentially in coding order through that periods last target, skipping untouched periods and unused tails; Decord uses its get_batch interface; TorchCodec uses exact seeking; Ours native uses sparse decoding (Section 3.1). LeRobot v3 [3] uses two-frame-GOP AV1 and TorchCodec approximate seeking. JPEG groups independently coded, frame-indexed JPEGs by episode and decodes requested frames with Pillow. Ours-DDRA (H.264/H.265) combines the encoding configuration in Section 3.2 with sparse decoding, open GOPs, and intra period 32. The main comparison uses Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.8.0a0+5228986c39.nv25.06, PyAV 18.1.0, Decord 0.6.0, TorchCodec 0.7.0, Pylance 3.0.1, and LeRobot 0.6.1 sampling semantics. A.2 Reconstruction-Quality Calibration The loading comparisons use one quality setting per transcoded representation. Quality is measured against decoded source frames using RGB PSNR within each dataset, then averaged with equal dataset weights. Table 3 reports the selected settings: all are within 0.18 dB of the LeRobot reference. This calibration measures reconstruction quality, not downstream learning performance, and is distinct from the downstream training sweeps. Table 3 Quality settings and dataset-macro-averaged RGB PSNR for the loading experiments. Representation LeRobot v3 (AV1) JPEG Ours-DDRA (H.264) Ours-DDRA (H.265) Quality setting CRF 30 Quality 79, 4:4:4 CRF 16 CRF RGB PSNR (dB) 41.473 41.393 41.294 41.496 A.3 Timing, Aggregation, and Throughput The main loading experiment runs on CPU-only node with 16 cores and 64 GiB memory. Its PyTorch DataLoader uses 32 persistent spawned workers, batch size eight, prefetch factor one, and one decoder thread per worker. Each methodpattern run has ten warm-up batches and 500 measured batches, split 167/167/166 across RealSourceWorld, RoboCasa, and Table30v2. Loading time is the main processs wait for worker results, including remote I/O, index/reference-graph construction inside the decode call, RGB decoding, and metadata transfer. Workers decode requested RGB frames but return only compact validation metadata; full-image validation is separate. Consequently, these measurements exclude full RGB-tensor interprocess transfer, GPU/model computation, and offline representation conversion. 14 Mean and p95 loading times are first computed within each dataset and then averaged equally across datasets. In particular, the reported p95 is not the percentile of all 500 batches pooled together. Media payload counts complete encoded episodes, rather than only packets passed to the decoder. CPU use is the mean number of occupied cores during the measured window, averaged across the four access patterns for Table 1. Table 2 reports average batch-loading time as Step (s) and average reconstructed frames per sampled episode as Frames/ep. All three configurations use H.265 with TI = 32 and ten requested frames per camera. Sequential takes the coding-order prefix within each requested intra period; Sparse and DDRA reconstruct their respective dependency closures. Shared frames, including boundary anchors, count once per camera per request, with no cache across requests. Frames/ep sums reconstruction across an episodes cameras and is reported to one decimal place; it excludes state-only parsing and has no batch-size multiplier. Using the values in Table 2, sparse decoding reduces Frames/ep by 47.060.5% and loading time by 32.955.4% relative to Sequential. Adding DDRA reduces Frames/ep by further 20.053.3% and loading time by 45.555.1% relative to sparse decoding alone. The combined design reconstructs 57.681.6% fewer frames than Sequential. Its loading speedups, computed as the ratio of Sequential to combined Step (s), are 2.73, 4.98, and 4.33 for Contiguous, Random, and Stride-4, respectively. A.4 Sparse-Decoding and Encoding Details SelectAndParse starts at the nearest random-access anchor preceding the earliest target in presentation order and parses through the last target in decoding order. If reference is unavailable, it retries from earlier anchors, ultimately retrying from the stream start. Each attempt initializes fresh header parser from the stream parameters. If no valid reference graph can be obtained, conservative contiguous path is selected before pixel decoding. In Algorithm 1, InitState loads the streams codec parameters and parameter sets into fresh decoder before replaying the validated segment. patched FFmpeg decoder implements the state-only path. The header pass maintains reference identities and buffer marking; the pixel pass repeats these state transitions with reconstruction enabled only for the closure. Overlapping execution ranges are merged, so shared anchors are reconstructed once per call. The closure-only equality applies to the validated sparse path. State-only updates retain H.264 reference marking, HEVC reference-picture-set handling, and decoded-picture-buffer bookkeeping without reconstructing skipped pictures. DDRA uses B31-capable libx264/libx265 builds, preset medium, CRF 16, yuv420p, and unchanged frame timestamps. The custom x264 build raises its B-frame limit to 32; stock build that clamps this count does not reproduce the configuration. Both encoders set keyint=32, min-keyint=32, scenecut=0, opengop=1, bframes=31, b-adapt=0, rc-lookahead=40, and ref=1. x264 additionally sets b-pyramid=none and aud=1; x265 sets b-pyramid=0. For frames, if (N 1) mod 32 = 0, the final frame is forced intra with -force_key_frames expr:eq(n,N-1). This closes the last interval without adding or dropping frames. A.5 Decoding Correctness We validate sparse decoding on 100 video streams from the evaluation corpus using 10,000 requests of ten frames each. Every request uses sparse decoding, and its output is compared against full sequential FFmpeg RGB24 decoding of the same encoded stream. The tests cover first and last frames, open-GOP boundaries, and duplicate or out-of-order requests. Outputs are compared in the requested order, including duplicates. All 100,000 returned frames are pixel-identical to their full-decode references, with maximum absolute RGB error of zero. Training-Performance Protocol and Additional Results Figure 4 reports thirteen VLA, thirteen WAM, and ten VLM configurations. Each family includes Original and H.264/H.265 DDRA at CRF18, 28, 38, and 48. VLA and WAM additionally include four LeRobot v3 AV1 settings; VLM includes JPEG at quality factor 80. Original uses the datasets stored visual representation 15 without additional transcoding: PNG for LIBERO and H.264 for the VLM training corpus. These sweeps evaluate task performance at varying compression levels, separately from the quality-aligned loading benchmark. B.1 Data, Training, and Evaluation For VLA, we fully fine-tune OpenPIs π0.5 on the 40-task LIBERO training corpus, containing 1,693 episodes, 273,465 frames, and two camera views. Original stores lossless PNG observations and occupies 32.5015 GiB. The Original and DDRA configurations use eight H800 GPUs, BF16, global batch size 256, and 30,000 optimizer updates. Standard LIBERO evaluation uses four suites with ten tasks per suite and 50 rollouts per task, for 2,000 rollouts per configuration. For WAM, we initialize from OpenWAMs pretrained WAM checkpoint and fine-tune it on the same corpus and compressed visual variants using OpenWAMs default LIBERO recipe [25]. The model couples Wan2.2TI2V-5B video backbone with separate ActionDiT through joint self-attention and mutual video/action visibility; the text encoder and VAE remain frozen.5 Each 33-step state/action window supplies nine video frames at stride four and 32-step action horizon. The two camera views are packed into 384 320 canvas (height width), with color jitter disabled. The training defaults use AdamW with learning rate 10 4, β = (0.9, 0.95), weight decay 0.01, and gradient clipping at 1.0. Training runs for five epochs with batch size 16 per GPU, one gradient accumulation step, BF16, and ZeRO-2. cosine schedule follows 5% linear warmup and decays to 1% of the initial learning rate; video and action losses have equal weights. Evaluation uses all four LIBERO suites with 50 rollouts per task (2,000 total) and rollout limit of 600 steps, extended to 700 for LIBERO-Long. Table 4 reports aggregate success rates for VLA and WAM using the same LIBERO compression factors. The displayed LeRobot v3 configurations use two-frame-GOP AV1 at CRF20 and CRF50 and VBR targets of 100 and 200. Their VLA runs use the full LIBERO corpus, 30,000 optimizer updates, and 2,000 Standard LIBERO evaluation rollouts. The VBR settings achieve compression factors of 93.375 and 188.224, respectively. For VLM, we fully fine-tune Qwen3.5-2B6 on fixed manifest containing 21,437 video samples and 9,706,740 frames. Each configuration uses eight H800 GPUs, BF16, ZeRO-2, AdamW with learning rate 10 5, global batch size 64, and maximum sequence length 8,192. Training spans three epochs, totaling 1,005 optimizer updates. MVBench evaluation contains 3,800 questions per configuration, with no reported inference failures. B.2 Storage Metric and Task Performance

sections.title: C Access and Resource Sensitivity Details
sections.content: The complete access/resource sweeps change one variable from ten contiguous frames, 16 CPU cores, 32 workers, batch size eight, and prefetch factor one. Requested frame counts are {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20}; fixed strides are {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; random candidate spans are 32, 64, and 100 frames. Batch sizes are {2, 4, 8, 12, 16}, worker counts are {8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64}, and CPU allocations are {8, 16, 32}. Reused common points give 27 distinct configurations, each evaluated with all eight methods. Figure 7 displays six methods and omits configurations with batch size two or eight DataLoader workers. Each point uses ten warm-up and 100 measured batches, split 34/33/33 across the three datasets. Statistics follow Appendix A.3. These shorter runs characterize measured trends, not confidence intervals; small nonmonotonic changes between adjacent configurations are not assigned causal interpretation. Increasing workers from eight to 64 at fixed 16-core allocation reduces DDRA H.265s mean loading time from 358.9 to 46.7 ms/batch. Increasing CPU allocation from eight to 32 cores with 32 workers reduces it from 132.6 to 71.1 ms/batch. The 64-worker point therefore does not require 64 CPU cores. These results reflect the combined I/O, decoding, and scheduling pipeline, not isolated decoder-kernel scaling. 17 Figure 7 Sensitivity to access patterns and loader resources. The top row varies requested frame count, fixed stride/temporal span, and random candidate span; the bottom row varies batch size, worker count, and CPU allocation. Each point reports average loading time over 100 measured batches, macro-averaged across datasets. Panels share linear loading time scale; lower is better.

sections.title: D Bandwidth Experiment Details
sections.content: The bandwidth experiment applies node-wide object-storage response caps of 20, 50, 100, 200, 400, and 800 MiB/s to all methods Lance reads from OSS through proxy with caching disabled. It uses the loading configuration in Appendix A.3, ten contiguous frames per camera, and the same deterministic episode sequence across methods and caps. Each run has ten warm-up and 100 measured batches, with measured batches split 34/33/33 across the datasets. Average and p95 loading times use only the 100 measured batches. Proxy throughput is total response bytes divided by elapsed time from iterator startup through worker shutdown, including startup, prefetch, warm-up, and shutdown. It therefore differs in both unit and accounting window from the episode throughput in Figure 1. The configured cap bounds available bandwidth.
